01 — What this document is

Three directions.
One decision.

A moodboard is a curated collage of images, colour references, typography specimens, and texture references that communicates a complete visual direction before any design work begins. It is how designers show a client what a brand will feel like — not what it will look like. The feeling comes first. The design follows from it.

Each of the three directions below is a complete, internally consistent visual world built specifically for Ember & Oak — the same brand, the same persona (Rohit), the same brief, but three entirely different answers to it. One direction is selected at the end of this document, with written rationale tied back to the persona and the design opportunity identified in the audit.

How to read each direction: The moodboard image shows the full visual world — photography references, colour palette, typography specimen, texture, and a single vibe word. The three-column strip beneath it breaks down the palette, the typefaces, and the atmosphere keywords. Everything is deliberate — nothing is decorative.

05 — Direction selected

Direction A.
Noir.
And why.

Each direction was tested against three reference points: the persona (Rohit — what earns his trust in 5 seconds on mobile), the design opportunity statement (warm within dark mode, method visible at hero level, scarcity explicit), and the competitive landscape (what none of the benchmarks do). Direction A wins all three.

Selected direction · rationale
Direction A — Noir
Why it earns Rohit's trust in 5 seconds
The near-black base and ember-orange accent communicate premium intent before he reads a word. Direction B's gold risks reading as generic Indian luxury — a visual language he has seen in five-star hotel restaurants across Bangalore. Direction C's monochrome palette compresses into an undifferentiated field at mobile viewport sizes, losing the atmosphere precisely where Rohit first encounters the site.
Why it closes the design gap from the audit
The opportunity called for "warm within dark mode." Direction A solves this through ember orange — the colour of actual fire. Orange is physically warm in a way that gold is not (decorative) and grey cannot be (cool). It differentiates from EMP's indigo and from Canlis's warm-but-light palette. No benchmark site uses this combination. It is the design decision the category leaves open.
Why Cormorant Garamond is the right display font
Cormorant Garamond at Light 300 creates editorial tension — refined and slightly fragile at display scale, which mirrors the experience of food that takes hours to make and minutes to eat. Libre Baskerville (B) is too heavy for a new brand without heritage. Playfair Display (C) is strong but sits closer to mainstream luxury. Cormorant's extreme thick-thin contrast is distinctive in a way neither competitor font achieves.
What Direction A commits to in every subsequent step
Base #0E0A06 · Accent #C85A2A (ember orange, CTAs and key moments only) · Gold #C9A84C (used once or twice for warmth) · Cream #F5EDD8 (all text, never white). Cormorant Garamond for all display. DM Mono for all labels and navigation. No decorative elements — the restraint is the design. Every decision must pass the test: does it make the fire more real?
Directions set aside · and why
Direction B — Ritual
The gold palette and Libre Baskerville combination risks reading as generic Indian luxury to Rohit — a visual language common to five-star hotel restaurants across Bangalore. The brand identity of Ember & Oak needs to feel like it could exist in London or Tokyo as easily as Bangalore. Direction B anchors it too firmly in a local fine dining aesthetic the target audience already knows.
Direction C — Smoke
The monochromatic grey palette is the most sophisticated of the three, but it creates a problem on mobile — warm grey tones compress into a near-undifferentiated surface at small viewport sizes, losing the atmospheric quality that makes it work on desktop. It also scores lowest on warmth, which is the primary gap identified in the competitor audit. A brand named Ember & Oak whose website contains no fire reference in its palette is disconnected from its own identity.
